11. Self-improvement by playtesting

Status: Experimental. Built in tools/playtest/ and run for three epochs in October 2026. The optimizer is an assistant session and the author approves every change; nothing is automated end to end yet.

11.1 Why playtesting can be automated here

Most self-improvement loops lack ground truth. This one has a good deal: the kernel knows the truth and the solution path, every event has a cause, and the scorecard can be computed from the event log rather than guessed. What it cannot compute (whether a game is fun, fair-feeling or confusing) is judged by a separate model against rubrics and is treated as weaker evidence.

11.2 Components

ComponentFileWhat it does
Text interfacegame.mjsThe game as a player sees it: places, people, things, questions, inventory and map, with opaque per-game handles (t3, q7, e2), never record ids. The real character pipeline and the morning director run as in the browser. A private trace records, per step, what the scorer needs.
Player agentsplayer.py, profiles.jsonclaude-sonnet-4-5 at temperature 0.8, a fresh context per game, a profile (beginner, amateur, pro: reading, asking, hint use, patience 20/40/80 actions) and a temperament; an in-character diary and an end-of-game questionnaire.
Runnerrun.pyBatches in parallel; --plan-from replays the exact episodes of an earlier batch (case, profile, temperament, seed) for a paired comparison. Budget: 100 actions or 8 game hours.
Scorecardscore.pySolved and correct, actions, hints, hints that helped (something learned within 5 actions), longest stall, loops, character fallbacks, declines, questions to the same person after a decline, rejected replies, refused actions, exceptions; problem records with their layer.
Judgejudge.pyclaude-sonnet-5: seven dimensions (challenge, frustration, confusion, character quality, fairness, liveliness, fun), each cited to the transcript; problems with layer and severity.
Reportreport.pyPer profile and case; problem clusters weighted by episodes × severity × profiles; paired differences with bootstrap 90% intervals.
Offline replayreplay.mjsPuts the same recorded free-text questions to two versions of the dialogue pipeline, without playing whole games.
Ledgerledger.jsonlFor each change: hypothesis, mechanism, prediction, refutation, then the result and the decision.

11.3 The method

Each epoch is one turn of the scientific method: observe (cluster problems and read their transcripts), explain (state a mechanism and check it in the data), predict (write the expected effect, side effects and refuting result to the ledger before running), design narrowly (a general rule, no case words or ids, the history the only source of facts), test cheaply (tests, parity, offline replay), experiment (held-out cases paired with the baseline, at least two seeds, one change per arm), and conclude (keep, revert, or explain anew). The gate requires all tests, generality, an improvement on the targeted metric, and no regression on the guardrails: correctness of characters, fairness, bugs and solvability.

11.4 Results

Training and held-out splits each have three cases (one easy, one medium, one hard) and three profiles; epoch 0 and 1 used one seed (9 games per split), epoch 2 two seeds (18 games per arm).

EpochChangeResult on held-out casesDecision
0baseline10% of character turns ended in one stock line, the same for every character; level-1 hints that named no one helped 26% of the time—
1in-voice declines and a rule against unbacked promises, togetherstock line 67 → 4, but solved −44 points (−67 to −22) and rejected replies +23 per gamerejected
2Adeclines alonerejected replies per turn back to the baseline (0.58): the promise rule had contradicted an existing prompt rule; players pressed the same person more after an in-voice decline (+0.72 of the next 5 actions, 0.28 to 1.11)superseded
2Bthe account the model chose, given as written, before declining; declines that close the subjectturns ending in a decline 8.4% → 6.7%; pressing −0.39 (−0.94 to 0.14)kept
2Chints that name whom at level 1 and the exact question at level 2hints that helped +35 points (19 to 53); judged fun +0.5 (0.1 to 0.9)accepted

Against the baseline, the three kept changes raise hints that helped from 57% to 87% with no guardrail lower beyond noise; judged liveliness is 0.33 lower (−0.67 to −0.06), which is open.

11.5 Threats to validity

  • Power. With 18 pairs only large effects on solve rate and judged scores can be seen (a 10-point change in solve rate needs about 100 pairs). Per-turn and per-hint rates are the measurable primary metrics.
  • Players and judge are models. Neither is yet calibrated against human play; the judge is close to the players' model. Reactions such as pressing after a decline may be properties of the agents.
  • Many comparisons. About 20 metrics per comparison at 90% intervals: one or two apparent effects per comparison are expected by chance.
  • Reused held-out cases become training cases over epochs; fresh ones are needed.
  • The offline replay is approximate: it rebuilds each state without the director, so people stay where the history left them.
